$$

$$

$$

So, the mass of the rod is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}+1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{3}+x]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}

$$

$$

We describe the mass distribution along a thin rod using a so-called **mass density function** $\lambda (x).$ This function tells us the *mass per unit length* at any point $x$ on the rod. The units of $\lambda$ are usually $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{m}.$

Consider a thin rod between the points $x=1$ and $x=3$ along the $x$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/c9/c9ee70d28476ebda61ccce5c6342a7f1a48a3e0f4dc26ee1af147d6f3d34a218.png)

 

Suppose the mass density function of the rod is given by

$$
\lambda(x) = 3x^2 \, \textrm{kg/m},
$$

where $x$ is measured in meters. What is the total mass of the rod?

To answer this, consider a point $x \in (1,3)$ on the rod and cut out a small piece of length $\Delta{x},$ as shown below.

![](images/9b/9b62c29b499159fe23e9ece7023ed179f4565600a88677fe51ab002a4a0d6faf.png)

 

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the mass of this piece is

$$
\Delta{m} \approx 3x^2 \Delta{x}.
$$

Note that the units of $\Delta{m}$ are 
$\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{m}} \cdot \textrm{m} = \textrm{kg},$
as we'd expect.

To find the total mass of the rod, we add together the masses of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta x \to 0.$ By doing this, we get

$$
m =  \int_{1}^{3} 3x^2 \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

 

Carrying out the integration, we find that the total mass of the rod is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\int }_{1}^{3}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & ={3}^{3}-{1}^{3} \\  & =26\,\text{kg}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given a thin rod oriented along the $x$-axis over the interval $a \leq x \leq b,$ if $\lambda(x)$ denotes the rod's mass density function, then the total mass of the rod is given by

$$
m = \int_a^b \lambda(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199490 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we saw how to calculate the total moment about the origin of a collection of masses distributed along the $x$-axis. We'll now extend our understanding to include moments of thin rods.

Consider a thin rod between the points $x=1$ and $x=3$ along the $x$-axis with mass density function $\lambda(x) = 3x^2 \, \textrm{kg/m},$ shown below.

![](images/c9/c9ee70d28476ebda61ccce5c6342a7f1a48a3e0f4dc26ee1af147d6f3d34a218.png)

How can we find the total moment of the rod about the origin?

To answer this, we once again consider a small piece of rod located in the interval $(x, x+\Delta x),$ as shown below.

![](images/fd/fd2dc58c503333a365b140de3ef1b559477788953dab14549478ca031df98125.png)

 

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can approximate this piece as a point mass. 

The moment of this piece about the origin, denoted $\Delta{M_O},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{M}_{O} & ≈x\cdot Δm \\  & ≈x\cdot \lambda (x)Δx \\  & =x\cdot 3{x}^{2}Δx \\  & =3{x}^{3}Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, to find the moment of the entire rod about the origin, we sum the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta x.$ By doing so, we get 

$$
M_O = \int_{1}^{3} 3x^3 \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

Evaluating this integral, we find that the total moment about $O$ of the rod is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{1}^{3}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{3(3)^{4}}{4}-\frac{3(1)^{4}}{4} \\  & =60\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

In general, the moment about the origin of a rod with mass density function $\lambda(x)$ for $a \leq x \leq b$ is given by

$$
M_O = \int_a^b x\, \lambda(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198496 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$

where

- ${M}_{O}={\int }_{a}^{b}\,x\lambda (x)\,\text{d}x$ is the moment of the rod about the origin $O.$

In our case, we have

$$

$$

So,  the moment of the rod about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{1}^{8}x\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{8}{x}^{2/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5/3}]}_{1}^{8} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(32-1) \\  & =\frac{93}{5}.\end{aligned}

We describe the mass distribution along a thin rod using a so-called **mass density function** $\lambda (x).$ This function tells us the *mass per unit length* at any point $x$ on the rod. The units of $\lambda$ are usually $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{m}.$

Consider a thin rod between the points $x=1$ and $x=3$ along the $x$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/c9/c9ee70d28476ebda61ccce5c6342a7f1a48a3e0f4dc26ee1af147d6f3d34a218.png)

 

Suppose the mass density function of the rod is given by

$$
\lambda(x) = 3x^2 \, \textrm{kg/m},
$$

where $x$ is measured in meters. What is the total mass of the rod?

To answer this, consider a point $x \in (1,3)$ on the rod and cut out a small piece of length $\Delta{x},$ as shown below.

![](images/9b/9b62c29b499159fe23e9ece7023ed179f4565600a88677fe51ab002a4a0d6faf.png)

 

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the mass of this piece is

$$
\Delta{m} \approx 3x^2 \Delta{x}.
$$

Note that the units of $\Delta{m}$ are 
$\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{m}} \cdot \textrm{m} = \textrm{kg},$
as we'd expect.

To find the total mass of the rod, we add together the masses of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta x \to 0.$ By doing this, we get

$$
m =  \int_{1}^{3} 3x^2 \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

 

Carrying out the integration, we find that the total mass of the rod is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\int }_{1}^{3}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & ={3}^{3}-{1}^{3} \\  & =26\,\text{kg}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given a thin rod oriented along the $x$-axis over the interval $a \leq x \leq b,$ if $\lambda(x)$ denotes the rod's mass density function, then the total mass of the rod is given by

$$
m = \int_a^b \lambda(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199490 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we saw how to calculate the total moment about the origin of a collection of masses distributed along the $x$-axis. We'll now extend our understanding to include moments of thin rods.

Consider a thin rod between the points $x=1$ and $x=3$ along the $x$-axis with mass density function $\lambda(x) = 3x^2 \, \textrm{kg/m},$ shown below.

![](images/c9/c9ee70d28476ebda61ccce5c6342a7f1a48a3e0f4dc26ee1af147d6f3d34a218.png)

How can we find the total moment of the rod about the origin?

To answer this, we once again consider a small piece of rod located in the interval $(x, x+\Delta x),$ as shown below.

![](images/fd/fd2dc58c503333a365b140de3ef1b559477788953dab14549478ca031df98125.png)

 

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can approximate this piece as a point mass. 

The moment of this piece about the origin, denoted $\Delta{M_O},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{M}_{O} & ≈x\cdot Δm \\  & ≈x\cdot \lambda (x)Δx \\  & =x\cdot 3{x}^{2}Δx \\  & =3{x}^{3}Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, to find the moment of the entire rod about the origin, we sum the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta x.$ By doing so, we get 

$$
M_O = \int_{1}^{3} 3x^3 \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

Evaluating this integral, we find that the total moment about $O$ of the rod is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{1}^{3}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{3(3)^{4}}{4}-\frac{3(1)^{4}}{4} \\  & =60\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

In general, the moment about the origin of a rod with mass density function $\lambda(x)$ for $a \leq x \leq b$ is given by

$$
M_O = \int_a^b x\, \lambda(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198496 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-66286cd3-980b-5dcd-96d4-d9a56bcaa6b2" :question/id #uuid "66286cd3-980b-5dcd-96d4-d9a56bcaa6b2"] ["question-66286cd3-980b-5dcd-96d4-d9a56bcaa6b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163014"] ["question-66286cd3-980b-5dcd-96d4-d9a56bcaa6b2" :question/problem "The mass density function $\lambda ,$ measured in $\text{kg/m},$ of a thin rod placed along the $x$-axis over the interval $1\le x\le 2$ is given by $\lambda (x)=4{x}^{3}-3,$ where $x$ is measured in meters. we'll learn how to determine the center of mass of a thin rod whose mass is unevenly distributed. 

We describe the mass distribution along a thin rod using a so-called **mass density function** $\lambda (x).$ This function tells us the *mass per unit length* at any point $x$ on the rod. The units of $\lambda$ are usually $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{m}.$

Consider a thin rod between the points $x=1$ and $x=3$ along the $x$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/c9/c9ee70d28476ebda61ccce5c6342a7f1a48a3e0f4dc26ee1af147d6f3d34a218.png)

 

Suppose the mass density function of the rod is given by

$$
\lambda(x) = 3x^2 \, \textrm{kg/m},
$$

where $x$ is measured in meters. What is the total mass of the rod?

To answer this, consider a point $x \in (1,3)$ on the rod and cut out a small piece of length $\Delta{x},$ as shown below.

![](images/9b/9b62c29b499159fe23e9ece7023ed179f4565600a88677fe51ab002a4a0d6faf.png)

 

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the mass of this piece is

$$
\Delta{m} \approx 3x^2 \Delta{x}.
$$

Note that the units of $\Delta{m}$ are 
$\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{m}} \cdot \textrm{m} = \textrm{kg},$
as we'd expect.

To find the total mass of the rod, we add together the masses of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta x \to 0.$ By doing this, we get

$$
m =  \int_{1}^{3} 3x^2 \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

 

Carrying out the integration, we find that the total mass of the rod is

$$

{:db/id 17592186199334 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199486 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to determine the center of mass of a thin rod whose mass is unevenly distributed. 

We describe the mass distribution along a thin rod using a so-called **mass density function** $\lambda (x).$ This function tells us the *mass per unit length* at any point $x$ on the rod. The units of $\lambda$ are usually $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{m}.$

Consider a thin rod between the points $x=1$ and $x=3$ along the $x$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/c9/c9ee70d28476ebda61ccce5c6342a7f1a48a3e0f4dc26ee1af147d6f3d34a218.png)

Suppose the mass density function of the rod is given by

$$
\lambda(x) = 3x^2 \, \textrm{kg/m},
$$

where $x$ is measured in meters. What is the total mass of the rod?

To answer this, consider a point $x \in (1,3)$ on the rod and cut out a small piece of length $\Delta{x},$ as shown below.

![](images/9b/9b62c29b499159fe23e9ece7023ed179f4565600a88677fe51ab002a4a0d6faf.png)

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the mass of this piece is

$$
\Delta{m} \approx 3x^2 \Delta{x}.
$$

Note that the units of $\Delta{m}$ are 
$\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{m}} \cdot \textrm{m} = \textrm{kg},$
as we'd expect.

To find the total mass of the rod, we add together the masses of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta x \to 0.$ By doing this, we get

$$
m =  \int_{1}^{3} 3x^2 \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

 

Carrying out the integration, we find that the total mass of the rod is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\int }_{1}^{3}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & ={3}^{3}-{1}^{3} \\  & =26\,\text{kg}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given a thin rod oriented along the $x$-axis over the interval $a \leq x \leq b,$ if $\lambda(x)$ denotes the rod's mass density function, then the total mass of the rod is given by

$$
m = \int_a^b \lambda(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3d97cfb9-13c8-5638-8080-e1c8cd1b90f2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7760 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "57e92bfb-7b99-5c98-ae8c-4999964eb518" :step/math-academy-id 44917 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199333}} {:db/id 17592186199346 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199490 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we saw how to calculate the total moment about the origin of a collection of masses distributed along the $x$-axis. We'll now extend our understanding to include moments of thin rods.

Consider a thin rod between the points $x=1$ and $x=3$ along the $x$-axis with mass density function $\lambda(x) = 3x^2 \, \textrm{kg/m},$ shown below.

![](images/c9/c9ee70d28476ebda61ccce5c6342a7f1a48a3e0f4dc26ee1af147d6f3d34a218.png)

How can we find the total moment of the rod about the origin?

To answer this, we once again consider a small piece of rod located in the interval $(x, x+\Delta x),$ as shown below.

![](images/fd/fd2dc58c503333a365b140de3ef1b559477788953dab14549478ca031df98125.png)

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can approximate this piece as a point mass. 

The moment of this piece about the origin, denoted $\Delta{M_O},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{M}_{O} & \approx x\cdot Δm \\  & \approx x\cdot \lambda (x)Δx \\  & =x\cdot 3{x}^{2}Δx \\  & =3{x}^{3}Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, to find the moment of the entire rod about the origin, we sum the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta x.$ By doing so, we get 

$$
M_O = \int_{1}^{3} 3x^3 \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

Evaluating this integral, we find that the total moment about $O$ of the rod is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{1}^{3}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{3(3)^{4}}{4}-\frac{3(1)^{4}}{4} \\  & =60\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

In general, the moment about the origin of a rod with mass density function $\lambda(x)$ for $a \leq x \leq b$ is given by

$$
M_O = \int_a^b x\, \lambda(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "23310936-fde8-5269-917c-4aec2c5591cc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7776 :tutorial/title "The Moment of a Rod About the Origin"} :step/id #uuid "459d7e8d-a9ee-5771-a2c6-38ae023189cb" :step/math-academy-id 45028 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199331}} {:db/id 17592186199347 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199491 :tutorial/content "A thin rod's **center of mass** is the point $\bar{x}$ on the $x$-axis where the system's total mass could be concentrated to give the same moment as the original rod. 

Analogous to the case of point masses, the center of mass of a thin rod with mass density function $\lambda(x)$ placed along the $x$-axis over the interval $a \leq x \leq b$ is given by 

$$
\overline{x} = \dfrac{M_O}{m},
$$

 

where 

- $\displaystyle m = \int_a^b \lambda (x) \: \textrm{d}x$ is the mass of the rod, and

- $\displaystyle M_O = \int_a^b \, x\lambda (x) \: \textrm{d}x$ is the moment of the rod about the origin." :tutorial/id #uuid "05cbd84c-3413-5883-bf92-6da730395e8e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7777 :tutorial/title "The Center of Mass of a Rod"} :step/id #uuid "a8a2d02d-5f5b-5ea7-8825-3d994a093207" :step/math-academy-id 45029 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199332}}] :activity/title "Moments and Centers of Mass of Thin Rods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198496} {:db/id 17592186199334 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199486 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to determine the center of mass of a thin rod whose mass is unevenly distributed.

To answer this, we once again consider a small piece of rod located in the interval $(x, x+\Delta x),$ as shown below.

![](images/fd/fd2dc58c503333a365b140de3ef1b559477788953dab14549478ca031df98125.png)

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can approximate this piece as a point mass. 

The moment of this piece about the origin, denoted $\Delta{M_O},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{M}_{O} & \approx x\cdot Δm \\  & \approx x\cdot \lambda (x)Δx \\  & =x\cdot 3{x}^{2}Δx \\  & =3{x}^{3}Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, to find the moment of the entire rod about the origin, we sum the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta x.$ By doing so, we get 

$$
M_O = \int_{1}^{3} 3x^3 \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

Evaluating this integral, we find that the total moment about $O$ of the rod is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{1}^{3}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{3(3)^{4}}{4}-\frac{3(1)^{4}}{4} \\  & =60\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}.\end{aligned}

$$
M_O = \int_a^b x\, \lambda(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "23310936-fde8-5269-917c-4aec2c5591cc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7776 :tutorial/title "The Moment of a Rod About the Origin"} :step/id #uuid "459d7e8d-a9ee-5771-a2c6-38ae023189cb" :step/math-academy-id 45028 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199331}} {:db/id 17592186199486 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to determine the center of mass of a thin rod whose mass is unevenly distributed. 

We describe the mass distribution along a thin rod using a so-called **mass density function** $\lambda (x).$ This function tells us the *mass per unit length* at any point $x$ on the rod. The units of $\lambda$ are usually $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{m}.$

Consider a thin rod between the points $x=1$ and $x=3$ along the $x$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/c9/c9ee70d28476ebda61ccce5c6342a7f1a48a3e0f4dc26ee1af147d6f3d34a218.png)

Suppose the mass density function of the rod is given by

$$
\lambda(x) = 3x^2 \, \textrm{kg/m},
$$

where $x$ is measured in meters. What is the total mass of the rod?

To answer this, consider a point $x \in (1,3)$ on the rod and cut out a small piece of length $\Delta{x},$ as shown below.

![](images/9b/9b62c29b499159fe23e9ece7023ed179f4565600a88677fe51ab002a4a0d6faf.png)

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the mass of this piece is

$$
\Delta{m} \approx 3x^2 \Delta{x}.
$$

Note that the units of $\Delta{m}$ are 
$\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{m}} \cdot \textrm{m} = \textrm{kg},$
as we'd expect.

To find the total mass of the rod, we add together the masses of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta x \to 0.$ By doing this, we get

$$
m =  \int_{1}^{3} 3x^2 \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

 

Carrying out the integration, we find that the total mass of the rod is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\int }_{1}^{3}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & ={3}^{3}-{1}^{3} \\  & =26\,\text{kg}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given a thin rod oriented along the $x$-axis over the interval $a \leq x \leq b,$ if $\lambda(x)$ denotes the rod's mass density function, then the total mass of the rod is given by

$$
m = \int_a^b \lambda(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3d97cfb9-13c8-5638-8080-e1c8cd1b90f2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7760 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186199490 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we saw how to calculate the total moment about the origin of a collection of masses distributed along the $x$-axis. $$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{1}^{3}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{3(3)^{4}}{4}-\frac{3(1)^{4}}{4} \\  & =60\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}.\end{aligned}

Analogous to the case of point masses, the center of mass of a thin rod with mass density function $\lambda(x)$ placed along the $x$-axis over the interval $a \leq x \leq b$ is given by 

$$
